planting.note: Divide the creeping rhizome into rooted sections and pot shallowly in a chunky, humid-terrarium mix; this Bornean understory species needs deep warm shade and resents both bright light and soggy soil.

directions: Begonia darthvaderiana is a compact rhizomatous species described from the rainforest understory of Sarawak, Borneo, grown for its glossy, near-black leaves with a deep red reverse that give the plant its dramatic, movie-villain-inspired name. Keep it in warm, humid, deep shade with consistently moist but fast-draining, chunky potting mix, since both strong light and soggy soil quickly bleach or rot the thin rhizomes. Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizome and grow it in a terrarium or enclosed case where humidity stays high, as it struggles in dry room air. Its low, spreading habit makes it a striking foliage accent among other shade-loving rhizomatous begonias in a collector's display.

planting.note: Root fresh stem cuttings and grow on in warm, humid partial shade in a chunky well-drained mix; this upright New Guinea species needs steady warmth and humidity to hold its spotted leaf pattern.

directions: Begonia brevirimosa is an upright, cane-like rhizomatous species from the rainforests of Papua New Guinea, prized for its large, puckered, dark green leaves heavily overlaid with silvery-pink spotting. Grow it in warm, humid partial shade in a chunky, well-drained mix, watering regularly during active growth but easing off once temperatures drop in winter. Stems can become tall and somewhat leggy over time, so pinching young growth and rooting fresh stem cuttings keeps plants full and well-furnished with its signature spotted foliage. It is best suited to a warm greenhouse, bright bathroom, or sheltered tropical shade garden where humidity stays reliably high.

planting.note: Start dormant scaly rhizomes shallowly in humus-rich, well-drained mix once warm in spring, keeping them barely moist until shoots appear.

directions: Smithiantha zebrina, commonly called Temple Bells, is a Mexican gesneriad grown from scaly rhizomes similar to Achimenes, producing velvety, dark-veined leaves and arching spikes of tubular orange-red flowers in late summer and fall. Start dormant rhizomes shallowly in a humus-rich, well-drained mix in spring, keeping them warm and barely moist until shoots emerge, then water and feed regularly through the growing season in bright, indirect light. After flowering the foliage yellows and dies back naturally; let the rhizomes rest dry and cool over winter and repot them to start the cycle again in spring. Because high humidity brings out its best leaf color and flowering, it does better in a terrarium, greenhouse, or humid windowsill than in open dry rooms.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and train the scrambling stems onto a totem or trellis in a humid greenhouse or large terrarium.

directions: Drymonia serrulata is a scrambling, warmth-loving gesneriad from Central and South American rainforests, named for its toothed leaf margins and recognized for the inflated, net-veined calyx that cups each tubular yellow flower like a small wine glass. In cultivation it is grown as a trailing or loosely climbing plant in a humid greenhouse or large terrarium, rooted in a chunky, moisture-retentive but well-drained mix and given a totem or trellis to scramble over. Keep it warm and consistently moist with high humidity, since dry air causes leaf edges to brown, and provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun to encourage flowering. Regular tip pruning keeps the lax stems from becoming sparse and encourages a fuller, more floriferous plant.

planting.note: Pot divisions or young rosettes in a well-drained, humus-rich mix and water from below to keep the hairy leaves dry.

directions: Streptocarpus primulifolius is a rosette-forming South African species with soft, hairy, primrose-like leaves and clusters of lilac-blue flowers held above the foliage, and it has long been used as a parent in breeding modern Cape primrose hybrids. Grow it in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich mix, watering from below or around the crown to avoid wetting the fuzzy leaves, which spot and rot easily when splashed. It prefers cooler, humid conditions and resents both scorching sun and hot, stagnant air, performing best on an east- or north-facing windowsill or under grow lights. Remove spent flower stalks and faded leaves regularly to keep the rosette tidy and encourage continuous bloom.

planting.note: Start small scaly rhizomes shallowly in warm, humus-rich, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm in spring.

directions: Achimenes antirrhina is a tender Mexican and Central American gesneriad named for its tubular, snapdragon-like flowers, grown from small scaly rhizomes in the same way as its more familiar achimenes hybrid cousins. Start the rhizomes shallowly in warm, humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring once temperatures are reliably warm, and grow on in bright, indirect light or partial shade with consistently moist soil through summer. Flowering continues through the warm months before the foliage naturally declines in fall, at which point watering should be reduced to let the rhizomes ripen and rest. Lift and store the dormant rhizomes in dry, cool, frost-free conditions over winter and restart them the following spring.
